events.what: Mouhib and Halbeisen prove HJ(3,3)>=22 and HJ(4,2)>=14 via symmetric colorings and SAT search
Conlon, Farnsworth and Robertson prove HJ(3;3)>=14 via SAT-extended van der Waerden constructions

judgement.doubts: The bullet asks, for each width, the smallest dimension in which X (first player, two-player game) has a winning strategy. HJ(3,3) is the three-colour Hales-Jewett number, which is not a two-player tic-tac-toe quantity at all; and even the two-colour numbers HJ(t,2) (draw-free dimension) only give an upper bound on the winning dimension, so lower bounds on them do not bound the bullet's quantity (e.g. 3x3x3 is already an X win while the draw-free dimension for width 3 is larger). Both 2026 events therefore settle or bound a changed question. If a later reader holds that bounds on HJ(t,2) count as bounds here, HJ(4,2)>=14 still would not, being a lower bound on an upper-bounding quantity. Researcher's own summary hedged on the colour convention ('or more precisely the 3-color... relevant to the 2-player'), which is where the misreading sits.

corrections.why: F13/F3: the record's events bound HJ(3,3), a three-colour Hales-Jewett number, whereas the bullet asks for the smallest dimension giving X a winning strategy in two-player tic-tac-toe of given width; lower bounds on Hales-Jewett numbers (which only upper-bound that dimension, via strategy stealing) do not move it, so both events are scope 'variant' and nothing survives; no pre-snapshot resolution is shown, so 'open'.
